title: The Great Dispersal
subtitle: Out of Africa for good, and the Neanderthal inheritance
era: Late Middle Stone Age; Middle to Upper Palaeolithic transition
summary: Between about 60,000 and 45,000 years ago one African population spread across Eurasia, mixing with Neanderthals for several thousand years on the way. Everyone whose ancestry lies outside Africa descends from it and still carries its genetic souvenirs.
narration: The survivors of those hard millennia did not stay put. Sometime between 60,000 and 50,000 years ago, a population from eastern Africa, perhaps only a few thousand people, moved into Asia. Earlier groups had made the same journey and faded away. This one did not. Every person whose family history lies outside Africa descends from it.

We know this because their descendants’ genomes tell a single story. Almost everyone outside Africa carries one to two per cent Neanderthal DNA, and in 2024 two teams dated when it arrived. Leonardo Iasi and colleagues, comparing ancient and living genomes, found one long episode of mixing, centred on about 47,000 years ago and lasting perhaps 7,000 years. Arev Sümer’s team read the oldest modern human genomes yet recovered, from Ranis in Germany and Zlatý kůň in Czechia, and reached almost the same date.

The first Europeans met Neanderthals face to face. At Bacho Kiro Cave in Bulgaria, people who lived about 45,000 years ago had Neanderthal ancestors only five to seven generations back. A man from Peștera cu Oase in Romania had one just four to six generations back. Yet these pioneers left few or no descendants among later Europeans.

What lasted was the inheritance. Neanderthal and Denisovan genes still shape our immune defences and our skin, and one stretch of Neanderthal DNA raised the risk of severe Covid for millions of people in 2020.

body.heading: One exodus that counted
paragraphs: Homo sapiens had left Africa before. A jaw from Misliya, a skull from Apidima, teeth from southern China and a layer at Grotte Mandrin in France record earlier forays (chapter 16). But the genomes of living people point to one later event. Non-Africans share the signature of a founding bottleneck; their mitochondrial lineages all fall within two branches, M and N, of a single African lineage called L3; and all of them carry Neanderthal DNA from the same episode of mixing. Geneticists therefore speak of a main out-of-Africa dispersal, usually placed between about 60,000 and 50,000 years ago, with earlier migrants contributing little or nothing that survives.

Why this dispersal succeeded where others failed is still debated. A 2025 Nature study led by Emily Hallett modelled the environments of dated African sites over the past 120,000 years and found that from about 70,000 years ago people began to occupy a much wider range of habitats, from forests to arid lands. On this view the emigrants were already ecological generalists, equipped for whatever Eurasia offered.

body.heading: Which way out, and where to wait
paragraphs: Two gateways were open. A northern route ran along the Nile or the Red Sea hills and across Sinai into the Levant. A southern route crossed the Bab-el-Mandeb strait, narrowed by low sea levels, into southern Arabia, then followed the coast or wetter inland corridors during humid phases. Both are plausible, and the evidence is circumstantial: stone tools rarely identify their makers, and genetics records populations, not footpaths.

A 2024 study in Nature Communications led by Leonardo Vallini and Luca Pagani offered a way around the problem. Combining ancient and present-day genomes with palaeoclimate models, it argued that after leaving Africa the ancestors of all non-Africans lived for thousands of years in a “hub”, most likely the Persian Plateau, whose mountains and valleys could support more people than the rest of Southwest Asia. People in Iran and neighbouring regions today carry an ancestry component that best matches this hub population, from which waves spread west and east over a period the authors place between about 70,000 and 45,000 years ago.

Genetics also hints at a lineage that stayed behind. The so-called Basal Eurasians branched off before the main Neanderthal mixing and carried little or no Neanderthal DNA. No skeleton has been assigned to them, but their ancestry appears in early hunter-gatherers and farmers of the Near East, diluting their Neanderthal share. Where they lived, perhaps in Arabia, the now-drowned Gulf basin or the Levant, is unknown.

body.heading: A genetic clock for the mixing
paragraphs: Neanderthal DNA works as a clock. Every generation, recombination cuts inherited chunks into shorter pieces, so the length of Neanderthal segments reveals how long ago mixing took place. In 2014 Qiaomei Fu and colleagues sequenced the femur of a man who died about 45,000 years ago at Ust’-Ishim in western Siberia. His Neanderthal segments were long, placing the mixture only some 7,000–13,000 years before his lifetime.

In December 2024 two studies sharpened the picture. Leonardo Iasi, Benjamin Peter, Priya Moorjani and colleagues analysed 58 ancient genomes from Europe and Western and Central Asia together with 275 present-day genomes. Almost all the Neanderthal ancestry in living non-Africans, they concluded in Science, came from a single extended period of gene flow between about 50,500 and 43,500 years ago, centred on 47,000 years ago and lasting roughly 7,000 years. They also found that “Neanderthal deserts”, long stretches of our genome with no Neanderthal DNA, already existed in the oldest individuals, so selection removed harmful variants within a few thousand years.

The second study, led by Arev Sümer and Johannes Krause in Nature, sequenced six individuals from the Ilsenhöhle at Ranis in Germany and the woman from Zlatý kůň in Czechia. They belonged to one small population, and the Zlatý kůň woman was a fifth- or sixth-degree relative of two Ranis individuals. Their Neanderthal segments came from the same shared admixture, dated to about 49,000–45,000 years ago. The implication is striking: until roughly 47,000 years ago the ancestors of all non-Africans still formed one population, and the split between the ancestors of Europeans and East Asians came later.

body.heading: Pioneers in Europe
paragraphs: At Ranis, bone fragments once too scrappy to identify were shown in 2024, by protein analysis and mitochondrial DNA, to belong to Homo sapiens. A team led by Dorothea Mylopotamitaki, Marcel Weiss and Jean-Jacques Hublin dated them to as early as about 47,500 years ago and linked them to the Lincombian–Ranisian–Jerzmanowician (LRJ), a leaf-point industry of northern Europe long attributed to Neanderthals. Isotopes from animal teeth showed that these people lived on a cold steppe comparable to present-day Siberia. Their genomes suggest dark skin, hair and eyes, and represent the deepest known branch of the non-African family: a group that left no known descendants.

At Bacho Kiro Cave in Bulgaria, Homo sapiens remains dated to about 46,000–42,000 years ago lie with Initial Upper Palaeolithic blades, cave-bear tooth pendants and bone tools. Genomes published by Mateja Hajdinjak and colleagues in 2021 showed that three individuals had Neanderthal ancestors only five to seven generations back, and that they were more closely related to later East Asians and Native Americans than to later Europeans. A jaw from Peștera cu Oase in Romania, about 40,000 years old, carried 6–9% Neanderthal DNA and a Neanderthal ancestor four to six generations back, as Fu and colleagues reported in 2015. Neither group contributed much to living Europeans.

body.heading: The Initial Upper Palaeolithic trail
paragraphs: Archaeologists track the migrants through a distinctive toolkit, the Initial Upper Palaeolithic (IUP): long, pointed blades struck from flat-faced cores, often accompanied by bone tools and beads. Its best-dated early appearance is at Boker Tachtit in Israel’s Negev, where Elisabetta Boaretto and colleagues in 2021 dated the earliest phase to 50,000–49,000 years ago. Similar assemblages appear at Bacho Kiro, at Kara-Bom in the Russian Altai and at Tolbor-16 in Mongolia by about 45,000 years ago, and at Shuidonggou in northern China a few thousand years later.

Many researchers, including Nicolas Zwyns, read this chain of sites as the trail of a northern dispersal of Homo sapiens across the steppe, and the Bacho Kiro genomes, with their East Asian links, fit the idea. Others caution that a technique can spread by contact and that most IUP sites have no human fossils. Europe’s other early industries, such as the Uluzzian and the Châtelperronian, raise similar questions of authorship (chapter 20).

body.heading: What the mixing left in us
paragraphs: Neanderthal DNA makes up roughly 1–2% of every non-African genome, and people of East Asian ancestry carry slightly more than Europeans. Denisovans added more in Oceania and traces across Asia (chapter 13). Archaic DNA is especially scarce on the X chromosome. A 2026 Science study by Alexander Platt, Daniel Harris and Sarah Tishkoff argued that this reflects who mated with whom, mainly Neanderthal men with sapiens women, rather than genetic incompatibility, because Neanderthal X chromosomes carry plenty of sapiens DNA from earlier contacts.

Some inherited variants proved useful. Neanderthal versions of Toll-like receptor genes and the OAS gene cluster shaped immune responses; others, such as variants near BNC2, affect skin and hair. The Denisovan version of EPAS1 helps Tibetans live at high altitude. Not every souvenir is welcome: in 2020 Hugo Zeberg and Svante Pääbo showed that the strongest genetic risk factor for severe Covid-19, a stretch of chromosome 3, came from Neanderthals and is carried by about half of South Asians and a sixth of Europeans. A protective Neanderthal variant on chromosome 12 was identified the following year.

Neanderthal ancestry even reached Africa. A 2020 study in Cell led by Lu Chen and Joshua Akey found more Neanderthal-like DNA in African genomes than expected. They explained it partly by later migrations back into Africa of people who carried Neanderthal ancestry, and partly by much earlier gene flow from modern humans into Neanderthals.

debates.question: Did the main dispersal leave Africa by the northern or the southern route?

views.label: Southern route
views.text: Supporters point to the short crossing of the Bab-el-Mandeb at times of low sea level, to stone tools showing that people lived in Arabia during humid ‘Green Arabia’ phases (a theme of work by Michael Petraglia and colleagues), and to the early arrival of people in South Asia and Sahul, which a route along the Indian Ocean rim would favour.

views.label: Northern route
views.text: Others favour an exit through Sinai. A 2015 genetic comparison by Luca Pagani and colleagues found non-Africans slightly closer to Egyptians than to Ethiopians; the earliest Initial Upper Palaeolithic is in the Levant at Boker Tachtit; and the Neanderthal mixing most likely took place in Southwest Asia, where Neanderthals lived.

debates.status: Unresolved. Later migrations within northeast Africa and Arabia blur the genetic signal, and both gates may have been used at different times. The hub model shifts the question: whichever route was taken, the ancestors of non-Africans seem to have gathered in Southwest Asia, probably on the Persian Plateau, before spreading. Dated human fossils from Arabia or Iran between 60,000 and 45,000 years ago would help most.

debates.question: When did the ancestors of today’s non-Africans leave Africa?

views.label: About 60,000–50,000 years ago
views.text: The 2024 admixture dates from Iasi and colleagues and from Sümer and colleagues require one non-African population still together around 47,000 years ago. With the earliest securely dated IUP (about 50,000 years at Boker Tachtit) and the ages of Ranis, Bacho Kiro and Ust’-Ishim, this favours a departure not much before 60,000 years ago.

views.label: Earlier, before 60,000 years ago
views.text: Archaeologists who accept an arrival in Australia by 65,000 years ago at Madjedbebe, and the 67,800-year-old hand stencil on Muna in Sulawesi reported in 2026, argue that Homo sapiens was already deep into Asia earlier. Some reconcile this with the genetics through a long stay in the hub, or through earlier waves that left little DNA.

debates.status: The genetic clock and some archaeological dates are in tension. Admixture dates depend on assumed generation times and recombination maps; luminescence and uranium-series dates have their own uncertainties. Most geneticists favour a main dispersal around 60,000–50,000 years ago. The Sahul evidence is discussed in the next chapter.

debates.question: Was mixing with Neanderthals one long episode or several?

views.label: One extended pulse
views.text: Iasi and colleagues and Sümer and colleagues find that almost all Neanderthal ancestry in living people traces to a single period of roughly 7,000 years, shared by all non-Africans before they diverged.

views.label: Several pulses
views.text: Earlier studies, such as Benjamin Vernot and Joshua Akey (2015) and Fernando Villanea and Joshua Schraiber (2019), explained East Asians’ slightly higher Neanderthal share by an extra pulse into their ancestors. Bacho Kiro and Oase prove that local mixing also happened later.

debates.status: Both are partly right. Later local encounters happened, but mostly in pioneer groups that died out, so they barely register today. The East Asian excess is now often explained by the dilution of West Eurasian ancestry with Basal Eurasians, who carried no Neanderthal DNA, and by differences in selection, rather than by a second major pulse.

sites.name: Boker Tachtit
sites.summary: Open-air site in the Negev that defines the Levantine Initial Upper Palaeolithic. Radiocarbon and luminescence dates published in 2021 place its earliest blade industry at 50,000–49,000 years ago, a likely marker of Homo sapiens moving out of Africa.

sites.name: Bacho Kiro Cave
sites.summary: Cave with some of Europe’s earliest Homo sapiens remains, found with Initial Upper Palaeolithic tools and cave-bear tooth pendants. Genomes show Neanderthal ancestors five to seven generations back and links to later East Asians.

sites.name: Ilsenhöhle, Ranis
sites.summary: Cave beneath Ranis castle in Thuringia. Bone fragments identified in 2024 as Homo sapiens tie the LRJ leaf-point industry to our species, and their genomes are among the oldest ever sequenced.

sites.name: Zlatý kůň
sites.summary: Cave in the Bohemian Karst where the skull of a woman was found. Her high-quality genome (2021) and her kinship with individuals from Ranis (2024) place her in the earliest known branch of non-Africans.

sites.name: Peștera cu Oase
sites.summary: The “Cave with Bones” in the southwestern Carpathians. The Oase 1 jaw carried 6–9% Neanderthal DNA and had a Neanderthal ancestor only four to six generations back.

sites.name: Ust’-Ishim
sites.summary: A human femur eroding from the bank of the Irtysh River yielded a high-quality genome in 2014. Its long Neanderthal segments helped date the mixing, and the man belonged to a lineage close to the split of western and eastern Eurasians.
